narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 64.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about you. Your class ranking at the end of your third year in law school was the strongest factor. Standing in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly the middle of the class among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 22.7 was the next most important factor; it sits well below the average of 37.2 among accepted applicants and also pulled the outcome toward not passing. Your family income bracket of Middle had a smaller but still noticeable effect. In this dataset, middle-income students are common, yet this category slightly nudged the prediction in a more positive direction compared with the other two factors.

Taken together, the model saw your lower academic standing in law school and modest LSAT performance as clear signals that the risk of failing the bar was too high to approve admission.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, seek academic support to raise your class ranking in future years, and consider part-time study options if they allow more time to master the material. With targeted improvement in these areas, your profile could look very different to the model on a future application. (248 words)
